turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Must you interrogate the poor man so? He is perfectly suitable, and I have already accepted his proposal – a most delightful proposal, I might add.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: My dear Gwendolen, your impulsiveness is, as ever, distressing. While I appreciate your enthusiasm, a young lady’s affections are a matter for careful consideration, not a hasty declaration. Now, Mr. Worthing, 149 Belgrave Square – a rather large number, wouldn’t you say? One wonders what sort of family could possibly occupy so extensive a residence.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, you are being excessively dramatic! Mr. Worthing is perfectly respectable, and frankly, his address is none of your concern; what matters is his character, which I assure you is impeccable. I simply cannot bear to witness such an undignified questioning.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: My dear Gwendolen, your championing of Mr. Worthing's character is, I fear, a touch premature. While I am not entirely averse to a gentleman with a certain… enthusiasm, *character* is forged in the crucible of experience, not proclaimed in a flurry of youthful exuberance. Now, Mr. Worthing, let us return to your family history; I find myself quite intrigued by this expansive residence at 149.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell, 149 Belgrave Square is a rather… substantial property. My parents, you see, are involved in… well, in various agricultural pursuits, and require a good deal of space for their operations. I trust that’s… satisfactory?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Agricultural pursuits! Really, Mr. Worthing, one would scarcely expect such a gentleman to be associated with turnips and manure. Do you cultivate them yourself, pray tell? I trust you are not one of those dreadful moderns who finds virtue in manual labour.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Oh, no, Lady Bracknell, certainly not! I wouldn't dream of it. My parents, they… they oversee the operations, you see, and I assist with… administrative matters, primarily. It's all rather technical, I assure you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Administrative matters! How very diverting. One assumes these 'administrative matters' do not involve, say, the tending of livestock or the, *shudder*, the handling of produce? I trust your pursuits are of a more refined and intellectual nature, Mr. Worthing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! Mr. Worthing is perfectly capable of discussing intellectual matters, I assure you. It is quite tiresome to have his admirable qualities dissected with such… *rural* skepticism.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Miss Fairfax, your interventions are… charming, but unnecessary. Mr. Worthing, let us proceed. I am most anxious to ascertain the precise nature of your family connections. One's ancestry, you understand, is a matter of the utmost importance.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, you are being excessively harsh! Mr. Worthing is clearly a man of excellent breeding and refinement, and I am quite certain he will prove himself most agreeable. Surely, a few turnips are hardly a reflection of one's character?

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Miss Fairfax, your enthusiasm is, as always, touching, but it does not absolve Mr. Worthing from the necessity of providing satisfactory answers. Let us not be deflected by sentimentality; a young man's lineage is not determined by the superficial observations of a young lady, however charming she may be.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: My dear Lady Bracknell, I quite understand your concern regarding family connections; they are, as you say, of the utmost importance. I am, truth be told, an orphan, discovered as a baby in a handbag at Victoria Station, but I assure you, I’ve always striven to uphold the highest standards of propriety and… and respectability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: An orphan, you say? Discovered in a handbag! Good heavens! It appears we have a rather… *interesting* situation on our hands, Mr. Worthing. Pray, do elaborate; I find myself exceedingly curious as to the provenance of this handbag and, more importantly, its former owner.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, really! A handbag? How utterly romantic! One simply *must* know more about this mysterious provenance; it sounds perfectly delightful, and undoubtedly explains Mr. Worthing's impeccable taste.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Romantic, my dear Miss Fairfax? Sentimentality is a dangerous indulgence. Mr. Worthing, a handbag at Victoria Station presents a most peculiar origin; I trust you have investigated the circumstances surrounding this... *discovery* with the thoroughness one expects of a gentleman?

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Indeed, Lady Bracknell, I have—well, I've made some inquiries, of course. It's all rather hazy, you see; the memories of the poor dear who found me are, understandably, a little… indistinct. I do hope this doesn’t reflect poorly on my character; I’ve always been a man of utmost honesty, despite… unusual beginnings.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mother, you are being excessively harsh! A handbag is a most agreeable starting point for a gentleman's history; it simply adds a touch of delightful intrigue. Surely, one shouldn't dwell on such minor details when faced with such an obviously suitable match.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Indistinct memories, Mr. Worthing? A most unsettling admission! One imagines a gentleman of impeccable breeding would possess a far more comprehensive recollection of his antecedents, or at least a plausible narrative to present to polite society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, I strive to be a man of impeccable breeding, as you rightly point out! It’s just that my… upbringing was, shall we say, unconventional. I am perfectly capable of crafting a narrative, of course, but I wouldn't want to mislead you with anything less than the truth, however… peculiar it may be.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Gwendolen, the carriage!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
